text: Look round at the courses of the stars, as if thou wert going along with them.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Look up once today, and stay with the sky for a minute.

text: The eye is the first circle; the horizon which it forms is the second.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
practice: Find the furthest point you can see, and let your eyes rest there.

text: Very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Notice one free thing outside that made today better.

text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then, or bear with them.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Be patient with one person who tries your patience today.

text: The only reward of virtue is virtue; the only way to have a friend is to be one.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
practice: Do one thing a good friend would do, without being asked.

text: If you would be loved, love.
author: Seneca, quoting Hecato
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius, 9, tr. Richard M. Gummere
practice: Show one person, plainly, that they matter to you.

text: When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Name one good quality in each person you live or work with.

text: Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.
author: Seneca
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius, 7, tr. Richard M. Gummere
practice: Spend some time today with someone who makes you better.

text: Hold every hour in your grasp.
author: Seneca
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius, 1, tr. Richard M. Gummere
practice: Pick one hour today and give it to one thing.

text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time.
author: Seneca
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius, 1, tr. Richard M. Gummere
practice: Notice where your time went today, without judging it.

text: Everywhere means nowhere.
author: Seneca
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius, 2, tr. Richard M. Gummere
practice: Close everything but one thing, and stay with it.

text: Nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Sit for two minutes with no input at all.

text: How much trouble he avoids who does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only to what he does himself.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Skip one look at what other people are doing today.

text: Look within. Let neither the peculiar quality of anything nor its value escape thee.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Look at one ordinary thing until you see something new in it.

text: Wipe out the imagination. Stop the pulling of the strings. Confine thyself to the present.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: When your mind runs ahead today, name what is in front of you.

text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things.
author: Epictetus
practice: Write down one fact from today, and the opinion you added to it.

text: Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed."
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Catch one complaint today before you say it.

text: Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Notice the thought you return to most today.

text: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,—I am rising to the work of a human being.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Do the first hard thing of the day before you think about it.

text: Set aside a certain number of days, during which you shall be content with the scantiest and cheapest fare, with coarse and rough dress, saying to yourself the while: "Is this the condition that I feared?"
author: Seneca
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius, 18, tr. Richard M. Gummere
practice: Choose one small discomfort today and ask the same question.

text: A cucumber is bitter—Throw it away.—There are briers in the road—Turn aside from them.—This is enough.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Meet one inconvenience today without complaining about it.

text: The art of life is more like the wrestler's art than the dancer's.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: When something surprises you today, take one breath before you react.

text: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
practice: Make something today without asking anyone's opinion first.

text: Insist on yourself; never imitate.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
practice: Do one thing your own way, even if it is slower.

text: Do your work, and you shall reinforce yourself.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
practice: Finish one small piece of work completely.

text: Lay hold of to-day's task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow's.
author: Seneca
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius, 1, tr. Richard M. Gummere
practice: Do today's task before you plan tomorrow's.

text: What I must do is all that concerns me, not what the people think.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
practice: Do one thing today without checking how it will look.

text: When thou hast failed, return back again, and be content if the greater part of what thou doest is consistent with man's nature.
author: Marcus Aurelius
practice: Do today's challenge at Easy. That is a return.

text: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
author: Seneca
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius, 13, tr. Richard M. Gummere
practice: Name what you feared about starting again. Then start small.

text: Nothing can bring you peace but yourself.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
practice: Begin with one small thing that is yours to do.

text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
author: Epictetus
practice: The missed days are not in your power. Today is.
